articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) on October 16, 2026. This action also included the publication of a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to provide further guidance on the updated authorization.

The specifics of the amendments to the General License and the content of the new FAQ aim to clarify permissible activities under the Venezuela sanctions program. OFAC regularly updates its sanctions programs through new designations, modifications, and general license issuances to adapt to evolving policy objectives.

Venezuela remains subject to targeted and sectoral sanctions, with specific entities, sectors, or activities restricted. OFAC has historically issued and revoked general licenses related to Venezuela's oil sector depending on political developments.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and a Cuban Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. This action also included the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on the updated sanctions.

The new Iran-related sanctions targeted 16 individuals and 11 entities, including financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies. Among the designated entities was Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), which was targeted due to its ties with Iran's Karafarin Bank, already under sanctions since 2020.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups, including Iran, to target the United States. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez criticized the action as 'aggressive,' asserting that BICSA is a legitimate bank with legitimate transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a Venezuela-related designation removal on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a specific entity or individual previously sanctioned under the Venezuela program has been delisted.

OFAC's sanctions programs are dynamic, with designations and removals occurring as part of ongoing policy adjustments. Venezuela remains under targeted sanctions, which restrict specific individuals, entities, or sectors rather than imposing a comprehensive embargo.

Such removals can signify a shift in policy or a determination that the designated party no longer meets the criteria for inclusion on the sanctions list. The details of the removed designation were not immediately specified in the announcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to counter narcotics and counter terrorism efforts on October 13, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities that threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy.

These designations are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to disrupt financial networks supporting drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally. The specific individuals and entities designated were not detailed in the initial announcement but are added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

Such designations aim to isolate these actors from the international financial system, prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them and freezing any assets under U.S. jurisdiction.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, International Criminal Court Designation, and Burma-Related Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This action also included a designation related to the International Criminal Court and a Burma-related designation removal.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, highlighting the agency's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions.

Additionally, the designation related to the International Criminal Court and the removal of a Burma-related designation reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, responding to various foreign policy and national security concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the extensive Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out specific permissible activities from broader sanctions, often to mitigate unintended consequences or facilitate humanitarian aid. The details of this new license were not immediately specified.
Russia remains subject to a complex array of targeted and sectoral sanctions, with OFAC regularly updating its regulations to address evolving geopolitical circumstances.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.

The Iran-related designations are part of ongoing efforts to pressure the Iranian regime, with OFAC having previously warned foreign financial institutions about potential targeting without advance notice if they transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions.

The amended Russia-related General License indicates adjustments to existing authorizations under the Russia sanctions program, which has seen frequent updates in response to geopolitical developments.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designation Removals, Updates, and Iran-Related Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designation removals and updates on October 5, 2026. This action also included the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related OFAC Alert warned foreign financial institutions that they could be targeted at any time without advance notification if they continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions. This alert is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' launched in August 2026 to cut off financial resources supporting the Iranian regime.

The amended Iran-related FAQ 156 clarifies how foreign financial institutions will be informed if OFAC finds they have knowingly engaged in sanctionable activity, removing previous language that suggested advance contact.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist activities globally.
These actions are part of OFAC's ongoing commitment to combating global terrorism by disrupting financial networks and limiting the ability of terrorist organizations to operate.
Designations under counter terrorism authorities prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in any transactions with the designated parties and freeze any assets they hold under U.S. jurisdiction.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty is part of a broader enforcement action against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

Bank of America agreed to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The violations involved channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowing designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, and failing to promptly update watchlists.

OFAC determined that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation.

OFAC's enforcement actions underscore the importance of robust compliance programs for all entities engaged in international trade and logistics to prevent violations of U.S. sanctions laws.

This penalty serves as a reminder that both corporate entities and individuals are subject to OFAC's enforcement authority and must adhere to U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a record $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread and egregious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This marks the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with its transaction monitoring system failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This resulted in the bank filing large numbers of late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars, many with indicia of money laundering.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance, with ongoing breakdowns in internal controls and insufficient staffing and expertise in its BSA/AML program.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express for AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank and its parent and affiliated entities for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance programs.

The OCC found that American Express's BSA/AML program suffered from systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training. The bank's risk assessment focused too narrowly on its demand-deposit business, failing to sufficiently address the risks associated with its much larger credit and charge-card business.

These deficiencies led to the bank failing to timely identify, evaluate, and sufficiently report approximately $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade. The OCC emphasized that banks of American Express's size and complexity must devote sufficient resources to AML compliance.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
